the knowledge of the individual may be considered as an "attribute" that is subject to human rights to privacy and security-of-person.

knowledge is a personal attribute and therefore should not be owned by an organization, but should be protected under the personal privacy or human rights theory, and that knowledge transfers and conversions should be based on ethical principles and the protection of the individual's privacy rights, and not on the organization's right to use its knowledge as a property right.
the ethics and self-interest of individuals and organizations are the counter determinants of knowledge transfers and conversions.

the ethics of knowledge transfers and conversions, and the ethical dilemmas that arise from them.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
knowledge is an asset, and that it can be managed as such; but it also is an attribute of the individual, which is protected by the human rights to privacy and security-of-person.

both the organizational knowledge and personal knowledge should be protected and that organizations have the right of ownership of the knowledge created by their employees while individuals have the right of privacy and security-of-person with respect to their personal knowledge.
both theories are applicable and that the use of knowledge transfers and conversions is dependent upon the context of the knowledge and the knowledge owner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ethical and moral issues in the field of knowledge management are not only complex and multifaceted, but are also very sensitive.
the knowledge management community should take into account the human rights perspective when developing and using organizational knowledge.
organizations should be allowed to use their employees’ knowledge as they wish, as long as they respect the employees’ privacy and personal security rights.
The main takeaway from our work is that
knowledge transfers and conversions may be subject to ethical dilemmas, depending on whether knowledge is viewed as property or as a personal attribute.

knowledge management practices should consider both intellectual property rights and personal privacy rights in order to avoid the ethical dilemmas that can result from the conflict between the two theories.
organizations should consider both theories when managing their knowledge assets.
